sentence: We present the case of a 58-year-old man who came to the emergency room with intense eye pain accompanied by progressive visual loss in his left eye.
The ophthalmological examination showed a pigmented mass in the iridocorneal angle that protruded into the anterior chamber, affecting the iris.
The patient's symptoms were compatible with acute glaucoma secondary to said mass present in the anterior chamber.
Ophthalmoscopy showed a large, irregular-looking pigmented mass with more raised areas.
The characteristics he presented on the ocular ultrasound were compatible with a large ocular melanoma with diffuse extension.
Magnetic Nuclear Resonance (MRI) showed a mass with a 17 mm base that was discretely hyperintense on T1 and hypointense on T2, compatible with the diagnosis of choroidal melanoma (1).
The Oncology Service performed an extension study that ruled out metastatic dissemination.
Given the tumor extension, the patient's symptoms and the absence of the possibility of visual recovery, treatment by enucleation was considered (1,3).
Macroscopic visual examination of the eyeball, after its extraction, showed the presence of scleral invasion.

The patient evolved favorably, maintaining ocular motility and a satisfactory appearance with the external ocular prosthesis, maintaining a good quality of life, presenting only difficulty in performing daily tasks that required good binocular vision.

Macroscopic examination of serial sections of the eyeball showed a circumferential mass of endophytic growth covering practically the entire choroid, extending to the ciliary body and iris, corresponding histologically to a proliferation of spindle-shaped and epithelioid cells with broad, pigmented cytoplasm, oval nuclei with prominent nucleoli with a degree of significant atypia.
The number of mitoses was high, showing hemorrhagic and necrotic foci.
These pathological data confirmed the diagnosis of diffuse uveal melanoma, with perforation of the scleral wall reaching its external surface.
